label: text
text: COAL CONFERENCE DISPELS HOPES.

label: text
text: Both Sides Stübborn.

label: text
text: IMPORTANT MOVE BY NOTTS MINERS

label: text
text: The coal conference has broken down, both the owners and the miners adhering to their previous positions.

label: text
text: In Notts the miners have accepted the owners' terms for 7½ hours at the old wages. The Derbyshire and other Notts owners have decided to open the pits on the same terms.

label: paragraph_title
text: JOINT MEETING.

label: text
text: London, Aug. 19.

label: text
text: The conference between the miners and the coal owners—the first for two months—was held at the offices of the Mining Association in London.

label: text
text: Industrial quarters beforehand were mildly optimistic. They drew encouragement from the fact that the Federation had decided to approach the owners direct.

label: text
text: The officials of the Federation had previously conferred with the Trades Unions Congress Committee on the subject of further financial assistance for the miners. The conference lasted an hour and a half. It is understood that both sides adhered to their old positions, the coal owners insisting on the eight-hours' day, and the settlement of wages according to the "economic position of the industry," and district agreements: the miners insisting on a seven-hours' day and a national agreement, refusing "to budge on the question of wages until they had definite guarantees regarding the reorganisation of the industry. Reuter

label: text
text: The conference between the miners and the coal owners has broken down.—Reuter.

label: text
text: Statements from the Mining Association and the Miners' Federation, respectively, were issued this evening.

label: text
text: PRICE, $3.00 Per Month.

label: text
text: Separate Statements.

label: text
text: The former says that it appeared from Mr. Herbert Smith's reply to an invitation to indicate the miners' wishes that the miners' position on fundamental issues is unchanged. Therefore no purpose can be served by carrying on the appearance of negotiation which has no real basis.

label: text
text: The miners' statement says that Mr. Herbert Smith explained that an extension of hours was unnecessary for the successful operation of the industry. A national agreement on the wages question was regarded by the miners as essential. The Federation was prepared, after consideration of the measures for the reorganisation of the industry, to consider what wages was possible. He intimated that consideration of these things might lead to an application to the Government for some assistance pending the completion of the schemes of reorganisation.

label: paragraph_title
text: Owners' Policy

label: text
text: The Federation's statement adds that Mr. Evan Williams, for the coal owners, made it clear that it was useless to proceed, intimidating their intention to take full advantage of the Eight-Hours' Act recently passed and insisting on district wages agreements.

label: text
text: The Federation's statement concludes:—

label: text
text: "The coal owners clearly consider themselves the victors. They have learned nothing and forgotten nothing during the stoppage. We have no alternative except to urge on the members" of the Federation the necessity of stiffening their resistance to terms which mean abject poverty to our people and a scandalous lowering of the standard of living for at least a generation. We again appeal to the public for continued support of the miners, and their wives and children, as it is now again clear that the coal owners have no desire for a negotiated settlement but only the resumption of work on terms dictated by themselves.

label: text
text:
No More Parleys.
Mr. A. J. Cook stated: "No further negotiations with the coal owners are possible. We have not asked the Government to meet us."—Reuter.
Further Details of Policies.

label: text
text: Rugby, Aug. 19.

label: text
text: No progress was made at the meeting to-day between the Miners' Executive and the Central Committee of the Mining Association, which represents the coal owners. It was the first time that the two parties to the coal dispute had met for two months, and after an hour and a half they separated without arranging for any further meeting.

label: text
text: Official statements were after-ward issued by both sides.

label: text
text: The owners' statement recalls the men's request for the meeting and continues:—

label: text
text: Mr. Evan Williams, President of the Mining Association, invited the workmen's side to indicate the points which they desired to put before the owners. It appeared from Mr. Smith's reply that the only definite announcement which he was in a position to make was that the Miners' Federation adhered to their demand for a national agreement, for no extension in hours of work, for a discussion on wages only after an inquiry into re-organisation, and for an approach to the Government for a subsidy. Mr. Williams, in reply, explained why, in the view of the owners, it was economically impracticable to resume work on the hours or wages conditions in operation before the stoppage or to make a national agreement which could meet the individual necessities of the different coal fields. He further made it clear that the owners remained as strongly opposed to a subsidy as they had always been. In view of the unchanged position of the workmen's representatives on those fundamental issues, it was clear that there was no purpose to be severed by carrying on the appearance of negotiations which had no real basis.

label: text
text: THEN "THE HAT"

label: text
text: A great demonstration parade of Canton strikers is promised for August 25, to be followed by a process of “passing round the hat” for funds.

label: text
text: This much 48 conveyed in a report from Canton.

label: text
text: The sponsors of the movement are stated to be members of the Kuomintang Party. Principally, the object of the demonstration is to encourage the strikers.

label: text
text: For six days afterward, a number of organisations (including also a proportion of the fair sex) will be permitted to canvass the city for donations.

label: text
text: Medals will be sold, together with door strips (of paper), each certifying that the possessor is patriotic and has subscribed a certain amount for keeping up the boycott of Hongkong. "Rates" of subscriptions have been fixed as follow: For a medal, $6; door labels (big house) $1 and (small house) 40 cents.

label: paragraph_title
text: HEAT WAVE.

label: paragraph_title
text: CHAIR COOLIES. DEMAND MORE MONEY.

label: text
text: FAT MAN'S DEATH

label: text
text: How chair coolies who, by demanding a higher fare, indirectly caused the death of a fat man during the heat wave in Canton, is related in a vernacular report.

label: text
text: The victim lives near the North Gate and had a daily to the West Bund. It has precluded from riding in a riches by his stoutness. Ordinarily he took a chair, and paid $1 for the journey. On Sunday the bearers wanted $2, pointing to his bulk and the oppressive heat. A bargain was not struck when the would-be passenger offered $1,60 and he decided to walk to his destination.

label: text
text: His death, a little later, is attributed to an 'epileptic fit.

label: text
text: From Fatshan city, it is gathered that the highest temperature (in the shade) on Sunday was 96 degrees. Rain fell during the night, and on Monday morning the thermometer dropped to 88.

label: text
text:
After having been closed since the heavy rain-storm of July 19, the road to Castle Peak is to be re-opened from Saturday but care must be exercised as several portions are still under repair.—A notification to this effect appears in our advertisement columns today.
In addition to several wash-outs, the road was inaccessible by reason of embankments being washed away on either side of certain bridges. This has involved considerable work.

text: The round-the-territories round will therefore be completely open from Saturday.

label: paragraph_title
text: HARBOUR SURVEY.

label: paragraph_title
text: WHY IT SHOULD PRECED DREDGING.

label: text
text: "ENQUIRER" REPLIES.

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mail"]

label: text
text: Sir,—I was interested in the reply to my original letter on harbour sitting, or rather in the Government view, as gathered on enquiry by one of your representatives. The records of tides and certain depths which he was informed had been taken since the issue of the Fitzmaurice report were not, as he was given to believe, part of the scheme of taking a general survey of the harbour, as recommended by Sir William. I have some knowledge of the subject and I assert that the only records taken were those in connection with works put in hand, records which would have to be taken as they were a vital part of such work.

label: text
text: Why have a survey at all? Why not get on with the dredging that requires to be done straight away? These are questions which rise to the mind of those unacquainted with this sort of work. But dredging done without proper data may—and probably would—be waste of time and money. A record on the lines advocated by the Fitzwilliam report would show where dredging would be attended by best results and might obviate the necessity of dredging certain places if the report showed it possible to direct certain currents to scour out such places by means of proper channelling and maintain them permanently clear without incurring further expense.

label: text
text: This might be possible in the case of the shoal off Kowloon Clock Tower and certain other places where silting has been in progress for a number of years. There are two shoals, however, which might be removed at once without any great difficulty by means of dredging and which need no harbour survey to indicate the way. These are the two off North Point—"Belcher's Ridge" and "Ramblers Shoal." The cost of removing these would be comparatively small and the operation could be performed within a week or so. At present

label: text
text: they constitute a great danger to shipping as any one who observes the manoeuvres ships have to adopt in passing between them can well understand. It would be a comparatively simple operation to remove them and make the whole fairway navigable at this point.

label: text
text: At present, although the carrying of pilots is not compulsory by law it is practically imperative in the interests of ship-owners with vessels entering the harbour that they should engage pilots. Such a consideration makes all the difference sometimes as to whether shipping owners direct their vessels to enter Hongkong harbour or proceed past it on their voyage. If it is only a question of fuelling or replenishing water supplies, the cost of a pilot may—and often does—determine them in favour of omitting Hongkong whereas if entry of the harbour without a pilot was a safe procedure they would direct the ship to enter here and Hongkong would get the benefit of certain harbour dues which it has to do without in many cases at present.

label: text
text: It is in the immediate—and infinitely more in the future—interests of Hongkong that a survey and improvements to the harbour are put in hand at the earliest possible moment.

label: text
text: Yours, etc.

label: text
text: Hongkong, August 19.

text: ALLEGED MURDER.

label: paragraph_title
text: VICTIM "CARRIED IN A BASKET."

label: text
text: CONDUCT QUESTIONED.

label: text
text: Questions were asked at the continuation of the Aberdeen alleged murder trial this morning as to the deceased woman having been taken from the house in a basket, whilst still alive; and afterwards sent back again.

label: text
text: A police constable who went to the scene in consequence of a report made at theกวมนิตยส์กอมกีเหลือกจำนวนจัดการของกว

label: text
text:
In reply to further questions, witness said that it was about 150 yards from the house in question to the police station. Just as the party carrying the woman got to the police station they met Inspector James who instructed them to take the woman back to the house. They did so.
Acting Sub-Inspector James, in charge of Aberdeen, "gave evidence. When he met the party carrying the woman, he said, he felt the woman's pulse, looked for signs of breath, and finding none ordered her return to the house.

label: paragraph_title
text: Material Question.

label: text
text: 'Questioned' by Mr. Hing-shing Lo, counsel for defence, as to why he ordered the woman to be taken 'back,' "witness'replied' that the question as to what position she was found in might have proved very material.

label: text
text: Inspector James also gave evidence of giving instructions to have the woman removed to the Government Civil Hospital and of finding in the room the chisel with which it is alleged that prisoner attacked his wife. Witness referred to the fact that there was a lot of blood about, on the walls, in the passage and underneath the bed.

label: text
text: Mr. Lo was questioning witness as to whether he could say by what “mysterious process” blood could have dripped in places other than the pool to which witness had referred earlier in his evidence, when His Lordship interrupted and said he did not think the Inspector could be expected to give theories regarding “mysterious processes.”

label: text
text: Mr. Lo asked witness if he was not more expert on tracing these sort of things than "for instance he (Mr. Lo) "would be.

label: text
text: Witness: No more than the verage police officer.

label: text
text: Husband's Conduct.

label: text
text: Two Chinese women, who lived in the same house, spoke of hearing the deceased woman cry out when examined yesterday afternoon at the Criminal Sessions hearing of a charge of murder brought against the husband. The prisoner disappeared, and a few minutes later the deceased woman was found in a state of collapse and bleeding profusely from a wound in her neck.

label: text
text: The first witness said that she heard she deceased woman cry out "save life". When she got to her, the prisoner was going down the stairs. "I followed him," she added, "because I was afraid he would run away." She asked him to return with her to help to stop the bleeding, but he refused to return.

label: text
text: Replying to defending Counsel, witness said that she distinctly heard the deceased woman use the words "save life". It was pointed out to her that other witnesses had said the woman shouted aish yah. She replied that she did not hear that expression.

label: text
text: The other witness said that she lived in the same house, and was awakened early on the morning of June 21, by hearing a noise in another room. She called out "what are you doing: are you fighting?" She had no reply, and on entering the room, she found the woman bleeding from a wound in her throat.

label: text
text: The case was adjourned until to-day
